title: Fridge and freezer during a power cut
summary: Know how long food stays safe.
steps: Keep the doors closed as much as possible.
Fridge: food stays safe for about 4 hours with the door closed.
Full freezer: about 48 hours; half full: about 24 hours.
Eat fresh food from the fridge first, then from the freezer, and keep canned food for last.
Throw away meat, fish, dairy and leftovers kept above 4 °C for more than 2 hours.
warnings: When in doubt, throw it out: smell and appearance are not enough to detect dangerous bacteria.

title: Organise and ration your supplies
summary: Make food last without weakening yourself.
steps: Take stock of what is available and how many people there are.
Eat whatever spoils quickly first.
Aim for regular meals at least: an adult at rest can manage with less food, but not less water.
Reduce physical effort to lower your needs.
Without enough water, avoid very salty or high-protein foods, which increase thirst.

title: Wild plants and mushrooms: be careful
summary: Never eat anything you cannot identify with certainty.
steps: Only eat plants you know perfectly (e.g. cooked nettles, dandelion, blackberries).
Never eat a wild mushroom without a certain identification by an expert.
Prefer stored supplies, known fruit and fishing over risky experiments.
Cook whatever can be cooked.
warnings: Some deadly plants and mushrooms look like edible species.
In a short-term survival situation, poisoning is far more dangerous than hunger.

title: Build a two-week food stock
summary: Foods that keep, can be eaten without cooking or cook quickly.
steps: Canned ready meals, vegetables, fish, meat (can be eaten cold).
Quick-cooking starches: couscous, oats, thin pasta, instant mashed potato.
Biscuits, crispbread, crackers, cereal bars.
Dried fruit, nuts, peanut butter, chocolate.
Powdered or UHT milk, sugar, salt, honey, coffee or tea.
Manual can opener, and whatever covers specific needs (baby, diet, pets).
Apply “first in, first out”: eat and replace regularly.
